newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRANCE MULLS TAX CHANGES TO HELP 98 BUDGET - PAPER.
newsitem.headline: FRANCE MULLS TAX CHANGES TO HELP 98 BUDGET - PAPER.

text.p: France's Socialist-led government is considering making permanent a rise in corporate tax and enacting other tax reforms which it hopes will make state revenues less dependent on economic growth, financial daily Les Echos reported on Monday.

The level of economic growth is a key factor in the government's decision making about the budget as it struggles to cut its deficit to three percent of gross domestic product to qualify for European monetary union.

Official forecasts predict economic growth of 2.8 percent next year, but few private economists expect that target to be met. Recent indicators have been contradictory, casting doubt on whether economic growth is speeding up.

Les Echos reported without citing sources that the decision would cover rises in the corporate tax and the tax on capital gains announced on July 21 as part of a deficit-reduction plan to cut the budget shortfall toward three percent.

The paper's report came just days after Prime Minister Lionel Jospin wrapped up on Friday negotiations about the spending side of the 1998 budget with ministers. He was planning to start work on the revenue side later this month.
Government sources have said that Jospin wants to keep the budget's spending increases to no more than inflation, forcast at around 1.2 percent next year.

The paper said other tax reforms under discussion included shifting employer payroll charges onto a broad-based income tax, called the CSG, and freezing income tax cuts voted by the previous conservative government. Such a freeze would save 12.5 billion francs, the paper said.
The government is also studying a reorganisation of the wealth tax, the paper said.
